Let coordinates on \(E\) be column vectors in the basis \(e_1,\dots,e_4\), and write
\[
p_t=(1,t,t^2,t^3)^T,\qquad v_t=p_t\text{ in }E.
\]

Since \(L\cap F=0\), every such \(L\) is the graph of a linear map \(S:E\to F\). The graph is Lagrangian exactly when \(S\) is symmetric. The condition \(\jmath(L)=L\) forces \(S\) to commute with
\[
D=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,-1),
\]
so \(s_{ij}=0\) whenever \(i,j\) have opposite parity. Together with \(s_{11}=s_{44}=1\), every allowed \(S\) has the form
\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&a&0\\
0&c&0&d\\
a&0&b&0\\
0&d&0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad a,b,c,d\in\mathbb F_q.
\]

For \(y=x+Sx\in L\), decompose relative to the symplectic pair \((v_t,f_1)\). Since
\[
\omega(y,f_1)=x_1,\qquad \omega(v_t,y)=p_t^T Sx,
\]
the \(E\)-component of \(\rho_t(y)\) is
\[
x-\bigl(x_1+p_t^T Sx\bigr)p_t.
\]
Thus \(\rho_t(L)\cap F=0\) iff this linear map on \(E\) is invertible. By the rank-one determinant formula, its determinant is
\[
1-\bigl(1+p_t^TSp_t\bigr)=-p_t^TSp_t.
\]
Hence we need
\[
p_t^TSp_t\ne 0
\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb F_q.
\]

Now, in characteristic \(3\),
\[
p_t^TSp_t
=t^6+(b+2d)t^4+(c+2a)t^2+1.
\]
Put
\[
A=b+2d,\qquad B=c+2a.
\]
For each pair \((A,B)\), there are exactly \(q^2\) choices of \((a,b,c,d)\). Therefore
\[
M_r=q^2 N,
\]
where \(N\) is the number of pairs \((A,B)\in\mathbb F_q^2\) such that
\[
u^3+Au^2+Bu+1\ne 0
\]
for every nonzero square \(u=t^2\).

Let \(R\subset\mathbb F_q^\times\) be the set of nonzero squares, so
\[
|R|=n=\frac{q-1}{2}.
\]
For fixed \(u\in R\), the condition that \(u\) is a root is the affine line
\[
uA+B=-u^2-u^{-1}
\]
in the \((A,B)\)-plane. Distinct \(u\)'s give distinct slopes, so any two such root conditions determine a unique \((A,B)\). Three distinct square roots \(u_1,u_2,u_3\in R\) occur exactly when the cubic is
\[
(X-u_1)(X-u_2)(X-u_3),
\]
whose constant term is \(-u_1u_2u_3\). Since the constant term must be \(1\), this requires
\[
u_1u_2u_3=-1.
\]

By inclusion-exclusion,
\[
N=q^2-nq+\binom n2-T,
\]
where \(T\) is the number of three-element subsets of \(R\) with product \(-1\).

If \(r\) is odd, then \(q\equiv 3\pmod 4\), so \(-1\) is not a square. Since products of elements of \(R\) are squares, \(T=0\). Thus
\[
N=q^2-\frac{q-1}{2}q+\binom{(q-1)/2}{2}
=\frac{5q^2+3}{8}.
\]

If \(r\) is even, then \(-1\in R\). The group \(R\) is cyclic of order \(n=(q-1)/2\). The number of ordered triples \((x,y,z)\in R^3\) with \(xyz=-1\) is \(n^2\). Among these, triples with a repeated coordinate number
\[
3n-2m,
\]
where \(m\) is the number of solutions of \(x^3=-1\) in \(R\). Since \(3\nmid n\), the cube map on \(R\) is bijective, so \(m=1\). Hence the number of ordered triples with distinct coordinates is
\[
n^2-3n+2,
\]
and therefore
\[
T=\frac{n^2-3n+2}{6}=\frac{(q-3)(q-5)}{24}.
\]
So
\[
N=\frac{5q^2+3}{8}-\frac{(q-3)(q-5)}{24}
=\frac{7q^2+4q-3}{12}.
\]

Therefore, with \(q=3^r\),
\[
\boxed{
M_r=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{q^2(5q^2+3)}{8},& r\ \text{odd},\\[6pt]
\dfrac{q^2(7q^2+4q-3)}{12},& r\ \text{even}.
\end{cases}
}
\]
